title: Sorry skeletons are the multi-agent protocol
intent: State the theorem-scale decomposition as an explicit multi-agent workflow: one pass states the target and the lemmas written for it, together with their API, as compiling `sorry` stubs; the statements are then frozen as interface, and independent agents each discharge one stub with no shared context beyond the file.

children.name: compile-before-fan-out
children.statement: Every stub must compile before fan-out (`lake build` on the skeleton).
children.closed_by: `lake build` on the skeleton — the whole sorry-skeleton must compile before any agent is dispatched

children.name: frozen-statements
children.statement: A filled sorry must not change any statement — statements are frozen interface; if a statement is wrong, that is a design change, surfaced rather than silently patched.
children.closed_by: the frozen-interface contract: a wrong statement is surfaced as a design change, not silently patched inside the sorry

children.name: many-small-stubs
children.statement: Prefer many small stubs over few large ones: the granularity criterion is 'one agent can discharge one stub without global context'.
children.closed_by: the granularity criterion — each stub is sized so one agent discharges it with no context beyond the file

applicability.goal_shape: A theorem-scale proof whose target and its supporting lemmas are not yet proved; the decomposition is the joint statement of the target and its lemmas as compiling `sorry` stubs with frozen statements, before any proof body exists.
applicability.use_when: you are about to prove a main theorem from lemmas written for it and want to parallelise the proofs across agents or contributors; the statements (the interface) can be settled before the proofs; and the team can compile the skeleton first.
applicability.avoid_when: the statements are still in flux (a change would be a design change to a frozen interface, surfaced not patched); the goal is a single small proof one agent closes directly without decomposition; or the skeleton cannot be made to compile first.

consequences: Freezing statements as interface makes any statement change an explicit design change that must be surfaced rather than silently patched — the price of the independence the workflow buys. The compile-before-fan-out gate means the skeleton must build before any agent is dispatched, so a skeleton that does not compile blocks the whole fan-out. The granularity criterion ('one agent can discharge one stub without global context') sizes every stub: a stub that is too large reintroduces the shared-context problem the workflow is meant to remove, while many trivial stubs add fan-out overhead. The independence of each contribution rests on the frozen statements being correct — the proof assistant verifies each stub against its own statement, but a wrong frozen statement propagates to the assembled theorem undetected.
